issues.legal_issue: Minor contradictions, omissions, and improvements that do not materially affect the prosecution case do not justify rejecting a witness’s evidence.
material_facts: The appellants relied on discrepancies concerning whether the eyewitness had seen an earnest deed and what he knew about the arrangement for sharing the benefit of the land transaction.
The Court found the discrepancies trivial and unrelated to the core account of the killing.
The courts below had assessed the evidence and found the eyewitness credible.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancies did not undermine the prosecution case or warrant rejecting the eyewitness’s evidence; there was no justification for re-examining the lower courts’ credibility assessment.
issues.legal_principle: In assessing evidence, a court considers whether contradictions, omissions, improvements, or embellishments materially affect the trial. Minor discrepancies on trivial matters that do not affect the prosecution case do not require rejection of the evidence in its entirety. An appellate court is not justified in reviewing the credibility assessment again without justifiable reasons. The Court relied on Sunil Kumar Sambhudayal Gupta (Dr.) & Ors. v. State of Maharashtra, (2010) 13 SCC 657.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.minor_discrepancies_do_not_affect_core_c: The identified contradictions, omissions, or improvements concern trivial matters and do not materially affect the prosecution case.
predicates.lower_court_credibility_assessment_has_n: The lower court assessed the witnesses’ credibility, and no justifiable reason is shown for disturbing that assessment.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal challenges evidence on minor discrepancies that do not affect the core case and gives no justifiable basis to overturn the lower court’s credibility assessment, the evidence is not rejected for those discrepancies.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction may rest on the testimony of a single witness when that witness’s evidence is wholly reliable, and the witness is not shown to have a direct interest in securing the accused’s conviction.
material_facts: The complainant was the sole eyewitness and testified that the appellants attacked the deceased with swords.
The complainant was a business partner of the deceased and one appellant, and the defence alleged that he might benefit from the deceased’s death and the appellant’s conviction.
The Court found the eyewitness’s testimony fully trustworthy and found no basis to treat him as interested in the legally relevant sense.
issues.conclusion: The eyewitness’s testimony was sufficient to support the conviction without corroboration, and the allegation that he was an interested witness did not make his evidence unreliable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 134 of the Evidence Act, 1872 permits a conviction on the testimony of a single witness if the witness is wholly reliable; evidence is weighed for quality, not counted by number. A witness is “interested” in this context only if the witness has a direct interest in having the accused convicted for some reason. The Court relied on Kartik Malhar v. State of Bihar, (1996) 1 SCC 614; Rakesh & Anr. v. State of Madhya Pradesh, JT 2011 (10) SC 525; Vadivelu Thevar v. The State of Madras, AIR 1957 SC 614; Sunil Kumar v. State Govt. of NCT of Delhi, (2003) 11 SCC 367; Namdeo v. State of Maharashtra, (2007) 14 SCC 150; and Bipin Kumar Mondal v. State of West Bengal, AIR 2010 SC 3638.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.sole_witness_is_wholly_reliable: The only eyewitness gives evidence that the court finds cogent, credible, and trustworthy.
predicates.direct_interest_in_conviction_establishe: The witness has a direct interest in having the accused convicted for a reason beyond merely being a witness to the case.

issues.definition: If a criminal appeal concerns a conviction supported by a wholly reliable sole witness and no direct interest in securing conviction is established, the conviction may rest on that witness’s testimony.

issues.legal_issue: An alternative account that unidentified third parties committed the killing does not create reasonable doubt when it is unsupported by the evidence and inconsistent with the credible eyewitness account and surrounding circumstances.
material_facts: The appellants suggested that villagers might have killed the deceased following a dispute concerning payment for land.
The sole eyewitness testified that the appellants attacked the deceased with swords after the parties stopped their cars.

The Court noted that the proposed account did not explain why villagers would chase and kill the deceased while leaving the complainant and appellants unharmed, and the appellants did not provide details supporting that account.
The complainant promptly informed the deceased’s brother and lodged a report, and the Court found the eyewitness’s account credible.
issues.conclusion: The proposed alternative account did not make the prosecution case improbable or create a basis for disturbing the convictions.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the proposed defence against the evidence as a whole and found it unsupported and inconsistent with the credible eyewitness account and surrounding circumstances. It cited no separate statutory provision or earlier case for this factual assessment.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.credible_eyewitness_identifies_attackers: A witness whom the court finds credible gives a direct account identifying the persons who committed the attack.
predicates.alternative_perpetrator_account_lacks_su: The proposed account that other persons committed the offence is unsupported by evidence or inconsistent with the surrounding circumstances.

issues.definition: When a credible eyewitness identifies the attackers in a criminal appeal and the proposed alternative perpetrators are unsupported by the evidence, that alternative account does not create reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Concurrent findings of guilt should not be disturbed on appeal when the courts below have assessed the evidence and no cogent basis is shown for finding their conclusions improbable or unsustainable.
material_facts: The trial court convicted the appellants, and the High Court affirmed the convictions.
The lower courts had considered the eyewitness evidence, the prompt report, the medical evidence, and the recovery of blood-stained clothes and swords after the appellants were arrested.
The Supreme Court found no ground to regard the lower courts’ findings as improbable or requiring reversal.
issues.conclusion: There was no cogent reason to interfere with the concurrent findings, and the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The Court declined to re-examine the lower courts’ factual conclusions where they had addressed the factual and legal aspects of the case and no cogent reason for interference was shown. The judgment cites no separate provision or earlier case for this conclusion.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a criminal conviction.
predicates.concurrent_findings_of_guilt: The trial court and the first appellate court have both found the accused guilty.
predicates.no_cogent_basis_to_find_them_improbable_: The record supplies no cogent reason to conclude that the lower courts’ findings are improbable or unsustainable.

issues.definition: When both lower courts have found guilt and no cogent basis is shown to regard those findings as improbable or unsustainable, the conviction is affirmed.
